docs.content:
# Project Context: Chevron (C++) ## Project Overview [*Summary of what this project is and why it exists*] Chevron is a C++ **GUI application infrastructure library** that provides the non-business, non-domain mechanics required to build a well-formed modern GUI application. It centralizes ownership of application lifetime, process orchestration, and GUI runtime control, while also supplying foundational infrastructure such as window/view mechanics, memory management mechanics, and other structural facilities that applications typically need but should not have to reinvent. Chevron deliberately does not abstract or unify GUI frameworks. Users select a single GUI backend and interact with it directly, while Chevron supplies the surrounding infrastructure that enables correct lifecycle sequencing, dynamic view behavior, etc. Chevron helps remove much of the concern around the specifics of a GUI applications functional mechanics, and allows users to focus on their problem domain. ---
## Chevron Philosophy Chevron is: - GUI application infrastructure, not a GUI framework abstraction - Concerned with: - process ownership - application lifetime - startup / mainloop / shutdown - orchestration of the chosen GUI backend - general application infrastructure
- Not concerned with: - widgets - layout - cross-GUI portability at the user-code level
“Not concerned with widgets/layout” does **NOT** mean "Not concerned with dynamic view mechanics" **IMPORTANT**: Chevron provides application infrastructure, **some of which necessarily includes mechanics that surface in the GUI layer**. That distinction matters.
A Chevron user: - Chooses exactly one GUI framework - Includes and uses that framework directly - Writes GUI code exactly as they normally would (*except mainloop parts*) - Uses Chevron to scaffold the applications internal mechanics
Chevron may internally abstract backend mechanics only so it can support multiple backends as library implementations, not to give the user a unified GUI API. Chevron is a library that owns the mechanics of a GUI application, not the interface of one. ---
## Key Technical Context **Language & Tooling:** - Primary language: C++ 20+ - Build system: CMake version 3.25+ - Cross-platform targets: Linux, macOS, Windows **Architecture:** - Chevron owns the application lifecycle as a first-class concept - GUI frameworks are treated as runtime engines, not abstract interfaces - No attempt to unify or normalize GUI APIs across frameworks - Internal abstractions exist only where required to allow multiple GUI framework to be compatible with Chevron **Conventions:** - Doxygen comments on all functions, classes, concepts, global/member variables, enums, etc. - Doxygen file header on all project files - Clear ownership semantics (RAII where applicable) - Fail fast on incorrect lifecycle usage **Important Decisions:** - No widget abstraction layer (by design) - No “write once, run on any GUI” promise - User code remains idiomatic for the chosen GUI framework ---
## FAQ >- **Q:** How much control does Chevron take over `main()`? >- **A:** Chevron does **NOT** take over the entry point method, it is left to downstream user-code to manage the entry point method of an application with the facilities provided by the library. Chevron is designed to give the user better control over their GUI application, not take control away.
>- **Q:** Is GUI backend selection compile-time, runtime, or hybrid? >- **A:** GUI framework selection is a runtime decision. There is a possibility that a hybrid approach would be acceptable here at some point later, though the focus is runtime selection at the moment.
>- **Q:** How does Chevron interact with GUI frameworks that already own their own mainloop? >- **A:** Chevron's concrete implementations of a GUI framework runtime will retain the necessary wrapper that permits Chevron to have control over this frameworks mainloop. Non-negotiable, Chevron must be in posession of the mainloop and be the authoratative library that invokes said mainloop.

**chevron::process::AppProcess**

*Class Design Description*

# **What AppProcess Is**

AppProcess is the **process-level coordinator** that owns and decides *when* the GUI runtime exists and *in what order* the application moves through its lifetime.

**It is the conductor, not a musician.**

Every Chevron-powered application has exactly one AppProcess instance. It is the first meaningful object constructed and the last to be destroyed. It owns the only GUI engine the process will ever have, drives it through a strictly sequenced lifecycle, and enforces that no step in that sequence is ever taken out of order or repeated. Nothing about the GUI framework, the window infrastructure, or any downstream subsystem is visible to it — it knows only that an engine exists, that the engine is in some valid state, and that it is AppProcess’s job to keep it that way.

It is not:

- A GUI object

- A window object

- A dispatcher

- A service locator

# **Where AppProcess Sits in the Layering Model**

AppProcess is the outermost layer of Chevron’s three-tier lifetime hierarchy. It owns GUIEngine and is the only class in the system that drives it. Everything else in the process layer exists within the boundary that AppProcess establishes.

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

Nothing in the GUI layer may exist before AppProcess has initialized its engine, and nothing in it may outlive AppProcess’s shutdown. The entire process layer is nested inside this boundary. AppProcess does not govern the details of what happens inside that boundary — that is GUIEngine’s concern — but it is the authority that decides when the boundary opens and when it closes.

# **What Problem AppProcess Is Solving**

Without AppProcess, users would have to:

- Manually sequence GUI backend startup

- Manually handle error paths

- Manually ensure shutdown correctness

- Manually guarantee invariants such as *“you cannot start twice”* and *“you cannot shutdown before start”*

Chevron’s core promise is:

*“If the application is running, it is running correctly.”*

AppProcess is the class that enforces that promise.

# **Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)**

AppProcess has exactly three responsibilities:

- **1.  **Own the application lifecycle

- **2.  **Own exactly one active GUI engine

- **3.  **Enforce valid sequencing

*Nothing else. If a responsibility does not clearly fit into one of those buckets, it does not belong here.*

# **Lifetime of AppProcess**

- Constructed near the entry point (user discretion)

- Lives for the entire process

- Destroyed at process exit

There should be **one instance per process**. The mechanism for enforcing this constraint is an open question — candidates include deleted copy/move constructors with documentation, or a runtime assertion on construction. This is deferred pending broader decisions on library-wide enforcement patterns.

# **How AppProcess Interacts With a GUI Engine**

AppProcess holds and drives exactly one **GUIEngine** instance — the polymorphic interface contract between AppProcess and all concrete GUI backend implementations. AppProcess interacts with the engine exclusively through this interface and has no knowledge of the underlying framework.

## **1. Committing a Backend**

This is the first meaningful interaction.

Conceptually:

- User constructs a concrete engine (e.g. **chevron::wx::Engine**)

- User hands ownership to AppProcess

- From this moment on, **AppProcess owns it**

**Important rules:**

- Only one engine may ever be committed

- Committing twice is an error

- Committing after initialization is an error

*This step is about intent, not GUI initialization. No GUI work occurs here.*

## **2. Initializing the Backend**

This is where GUI involvement begins.

At this point:

- The backend is selected

- Configuration is locked

- No windows exist yet

AppProcess instructs the engine:

*“Okay, engine — initialize yourself, but do not enter the mainloop yet.”*

This gives the engine a chance to:

- Initialize the GUI library

- Validate environment assumptions

- Prepare internal subsystems

If this fails:

- No mainloop starts

- No windows are created

- The application can still exit cleanly

## **3. Starting the Runtime (The Mainloop)**

**This is the point of no return.**

When startRuntime() is called:

- The GUI engine becomes active

- Windows are materialized

- The mainloop begins

- Control flow is given to the GUI framework

- The call blocks until shutdown

From AppProcess’s perspective:

- This is a single operation

- It either returns normally

- Or returns an error code

*AppProcess does not care how the mainloop works. That is the engine’s job.*

## **4. Shutdown**

*Shutdown is not the inverse of startup.*

Key idea:

*Shutdown may be requested by either user code or the GUI engine.*

So AppProcess must support:

- Explicit shutdown calls from user code

- Implicit shutdown after the mainloop exits

During shutdown:

- No new GUI work is allowed

- The engine is asked to tear down cleanly

- Resources unwind in a controlled order

**Calling shutdown twice must be safe.**

# **What AppProcess Deliberately Does Not Know**

*This is just as important as what it does know.*

AppProcess does not know:

- What windows exist

- What GUI framework is in use

- How window dispatching works

- How widgets are constructed

- How events are routed

- How window registration is managed — that responsibility belongs to GUIEngine and is surfaced to user code through WindowingSubsystem via engine.windowing()

It only knows:

- *“an engine exists”*

- *“it is initialized”*

- *“it is running”*

- *“it is shutting down”*

# **Error Handling Philosophy**

AppProcess should:

- Fail fast on misuse

- Return explicit status codes where applicable

- Never leave the system half-alive

- Throw on exceptional code paths

**Note: **The precise boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions is an open question pending broader library-wide decisions on error handling strategy. The intent above captures the directional philosophy only.

Examples of misuse that must be caught:

- Starting without a committed engine

- Committing after start

- Initializing twice

- Runtime configuration errors

# **Public API Shape (Conceptual, Not Code)**

Without syntax, here is what the surface feels like:

- Construct an AppProcess

- Commit a configured GUIEngine

- Initialize it

- Start its mainloop

- Gracefully shut it down

# **Open Questions and Deferred Decisions**

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **One-instance-per-process enforcement: **The mechanism for enforcing this constraint has not been decided. Candidates include deleted copy/move constructors with documentation, or a runtime assertion on construction.

- **Error handling boundary: **The exact line between returned error codes and thrown exceptions is not yet drawn. This depends on broader library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

- **GUIEngine virtual interface shape: **The precise set of virtual methods that compose the GUIEngine contract — the exact signatures AppProcess calls through — is a development-time detail deferred to implementation. The broader design of GUIEngine and the process layer is established.

*Chevron Library — Internal Design Documentation*

**chevron::process::GUIEngine**

*Class Design Description*

# **What GUIEngine Is**

GUIEngine is the **owner of everything that is only valid while the GUI is alive**. It is the boundary between the process-level world that AppProcess governs and the GUI-bound world that the chosen framework inhabits.

Where AppProcess decides *when* a GUI runtime exists, GUIEngine decides *what happens while it exists*. That division is the foundation of Chevron’s layering model.

It is not:

- A GUI framework wrapper or abstraction layer

- A window object or window factory

- A service locator

- A business logic container

*It is the environment in which all GUI-bound infrastructure lives — and the authority that governs that environment’s lifetime.*

# **Where GUIEngine Sits in the Layering Model**

Chevron’s architecture is built around three nested lifetime layers, each owning exactly what belongs to it:

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

AppProcess is the outermost layer. It owns GUIEngine. GUIEngine owns everything that requires the GUI framework to be alive. Nothing in the GUI layer may exist before GUIEngine is initialized, and nothing in it may outlive GUIEngine’s shutdown.

# **The Core Invariant**

*If GUIEngine exists, the GUI framework is either initialized or about to be initialized.*

The corollary is just as important:

*If GUIEngine does not exist, no GUI-related object may exist.*

This invariant is what makes the rest of the system safe to reason about. It is GUIEngine’s job to uphold it, and AppProcess’s job to ensure GUIEngine is only driven in ways that preserve it.

# **What Problem GUIEngine Is Solving**

GUI frameworks are not passive libraries — they are environments with opinions:

- They carry global state that must be initialized before use

- They impose threading requirements that must be respected

- They have their own startup and shutdown sequencing rules

- They often assume they own the process and its mainloop

Without GUIEngine, each of these concerns falls on the user to manage manually and correctly. Chevron’s job is to tame that environment — to bring the framework under a controlled lifecycle rather than letting it run freely. GUIEngine is the class that performs that taming.

# **Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)**

GUIEngine has exactly three responsibilities:

- **1.  **Own and control the GUI framework environment

- **2.  **Own all GUI-scoped infrastructure for the duration of GUI lifetime

- **3.  **Enforce the invariant that no GUI-bound object exists outside of GUI lifetime

*Nothing else. If a responsibility does not clearly fit into one of those buckets, it does not belong here.*

# **What GUIEngine Owns**

At the base class level, GUIEngine owns all infrastructure whose lifetime is bounded by the GUI being alive. Critically, the majority of this infrastructure is **GUI-framework-agnostic** and therefore belongs at the base level — written once and shared across all concrete implementations.

This includes:

- **WindowDispatcher** — responsible for the act of window creation. Holds and executes the logic that produces new window instances when a window is requested. Does not manage what it produces.

- **WindowCoordinator** — receives ownership of what WindowDispatcher produces. Tracks all live WindowEnvelope instances, manages their relationships via WindowHierarchy, and is aware when the last window has closed. May signal shutdown as a result.

- **WindowingSubsystem** — the public-facing projection of GUIEngine’s windowing capability. Holds non-owning references to WindowDispatcher and WindowCoordinator and surfaces their collaboration as a coherent user-facing API. Accessed via the windowing() accessor in both const and non-const overloads.

- **WindowEnvelope instances** — each live window is represented by a WindowEnvelope that bundles the raw backend window handle with a WindowComponentStore carrying Chevron’s per-window infrastructure. Their lifetime is governed by WindowCoordinator.

Concrete engine implementations (wx::Engine, qt::Engine, etc.) own only what is genuinely framework-specific:

- The framework’s application object (wxApp, QApplication, etc.)

- The mainloop wrapper that gives Chevron control over the framework’s event loop

- Any framework-specific initialization or teardown logic

# **What GUIEngine Deliberately Does Not Own**

*This is just as important as what it does own.*

GUIEngine does not own:

- Application lifetime or process startup and exit

- Command line parsing beyond what the backend minimally requires

- Business logic of any kind

- Non-GUI services or infrastructure

That boundary keeps the layering clean. AppProcess governs the process. GUIEngine governs the GUI environment within it. Neither reaches into the other’s domain.

# **Lifetime of GUIEngine**

GUIEngine is constructed by the user as a concrete implementation, configured, and then committed to AppProcess. From that point forward, AppProcess drives it exclusively through the GUIEngine interface.

## **1. Construction**

The user constructs a concrete engine (e.g. chevron::wx::Engine). At this point, no GUI framework calls have occurred and no global GUI state has been touched. Configuration is still mutable. This phase exists solely to prepare the engine for commitment.

*Nothing GUI-visible exists yet.*

## **2. Commitment to AppProcess**

Ownership transfers to AppProcess. Configuration is effectively locked. The engine is now the chosen backend for the lifetime of the process. Still no GUI initialization, no windows, no mainloop.

## **3. Initialization**

AppProcess instructs the engine to initialize. This is where the GUI framework comes alive: the framework’s application object is created, environment assumptions are validated, and internal subsystems are prepared. The mainloop has **not** started. Windows do **not** exist yet.

If initialization fails:

- No mainloop starts

- No windows are created

- The application can still exit cleanly

## **4. Runtime Start**

**This is the point of no return.**

AppProcess calls mainloopEntry(), which honors the call by invoking runtime() on the engine. The engine materializes windows through WindowDispatcher, WindowCoordinator begins tracking them, and the mainloop enters. From this moment, mainloopEntry() blocks. Control flow is inside the GUI framework until shutdown.

## **5. Shutdown and Teardown**

*Shutdown is not the inverse of startup.*

Shutdown may be initiated by user code, by the GUI framework itself (e.g. the last window closes), or by AppProcess. The engine must support all three origins without the caller needing to coordinate them.

During shutdown:

- The mainloop is stopped

- WindowingSubsystem is destroyed before its referenced components

- WindowCoordinator winds down live windows in a controlled order

- Per-window infrastructure is torn down with each window envelope

- The GUI framework is deinitialized

- Control returns to AppProcess

**Calling shutdown twice must be safe.**

# **Abstract Base vs. Concrete Implementations**

The base GUIEngine class defines the lifecycle contract, ownership boundaries, and sequencing rules. It is the surface that AppProcess sees and the only surface it is permitted to use.

Concrete implementations inherit from this base and are responsible for exactly one thing that varies per backend: how the framework is initialized, how its mainloop is controlled, and how it is torn down. Everything else — window dispatching, window coordination, the envelope model, the windowing subsystem projection — is handled at the base level and is not reimplemented per backend.

Concrete implementations provide the framework-specific lifecycle behavior through the pure virtual interface defined by the base class. The pure virtual methods are the contract — they declare exactly what each backend must implement: how the framework is initialized, how its mainloop is entered and controlled, and how it is torn down. The base class handles everything else, including all orchestration of WindowDispatcher, WindowCoordinator, and WindowingSubsystem. Concrete engines do not reach into those components directly.

Adding a new backend is therefore a focused task: implement the framework-specific lifecycle and respond to the defined hooks where needed. The base class handles everything else.

# **Error Handling Philosophy**

GUIEngine should:

- Fail fast on lifecycle misuse

- Return explicit status codes where applicable

- Never leave the GUI environment half-initialized or half-alive

- Throw on exceptional code paths

**Note: **The precise boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as AppProcess — deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

Examples of misuse that must be caught:

- Any GUI-bound operation attempted before initialization

- Starting the mainloop without a committed and initialized engine

- Initializing twice

- Window operations attempted after shutdown has begun

# **Public API Shape (Conceptual, Not Code)**

From AppProcess’s perspective, the surface of GUIEngine is intentionally narrow:

- Initialize the GUI framework

- Start the mainloop and block

- Accept a shutdown signal and tear down cleanly

All windowing operations — factory registration, window dispatch, live window queries, component access — are not part of GUIEngine’s direct API. They are surfaced through WindowingSubsystem via the windowing() accessor, which is the intended entry point for all user-facing windowing work. AppProcess never touches this surface.

# **Open Questions and Deferred Decisions**

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **WindowDispatcher / WindowCoordinator handoff mechanism: **The precise protocol by which a newly constructed WindowEnvelope transfers ownership from the dispatcher to the coordinator has not been designed.

- **Shutdown signal routing: **The precise mechanism by which a framework-initiated shutdown (e.g. last window closed) is communicated back to AppProcess has not been defined.

- **Pure virtual interface shape: **The precise set of pure virtual methods that compose the GUIEngine contract — their names, signatures, and sequencing guarantees — is a development-time detail deferred to implementation.

- **Future subsystem projections: **WindowingSubsystem is the first instance of the subsystem projection pattern on GUIEngine. Additional subsystems — event routing and others — will be added as the library grows. Their design is deferred to the appropriate phase of development.

- **Error handling boundary: **Follows the same open question as AppProcess. Deferred pending library-wide decisions.

*Chevron Library — Internal Design Documentation*

**chevron::process::****WindowDispatcher**

*Class Design Description*

# What WindowDispatcher Is

WindowDispatcher is the **GUI-scoped authority for window creation**. It is the single point through which all window construction requests must pass, and it answers one question at the moment of each request:

*Is this window allowed to exist right now, and if so — create it.*

It is not a manager, a tracker, or a policy brain. Once a window has been created and handed off, WindowDispatcher is done with it. Its concern is the act of creation, not the consequences.

It is not:

- A window manager or lifetime owner of windows

- A GUI abstraction layer

- An event router

- *A one-time startup **mechanism — it** remains an active, callable service for the entire duration of GUI lifetime*

# Where WindowDispatcher Sits in the Layering Model

WindowDispatcher is a GUI-scoped component that lives inside GUIEngine at the base class level. It is not reimplemented by each concrete backend — it is framework-agnostic infrastructure that every backend inherits.

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)

                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)

                          |- WindowingSubsystem  (user-facing projection)

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

The division of responsibility between WindowDispatcher and WindowCoordinator is deliberate and non-negotiable: WindowDispatcher creates windows, WindowCoordinator owns them afterward. The seam between those two classes is where a newly constructed window envelope transfers from one authority to the other. Neither class reaches into the other’s domain.

# What Problem WindowDispatcher Is Solving

Without a centralized creation authority, GUI applications tend to accumulate the same set of problems:

- Windows are created ad-hoc from arbitrary locations in user code

- No clear policy exists around when a window may or may not be created

- Business logic becomes tightly coupled to GUI construction details

- There is no clean way to re-create a window that has been closed

- Startup window logic cannot be reused for windows opened later at runtime

WindowDispatcher eliminates all of these by making window creation a governed, centralized act. User code declares window intent by registering factories. The dispatcher is the only thing that ever executes those factories, and only when the conditions are right.

# Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)

WindowDispatcher has exactly four responsibilities:

- **1****.  **Accept window factory registrations as declarative intent

- **2****.  **Store and manage WindowFactory instances that pair each factory with its descriptor

- **3****.  **Materialize windows on demand by executing the appropriate factory at the right moment

- **4****.  **Hand off newly created window envelopes to WindowCoordinator and relinquish all further involvement

That fourth responsibility is as important as any of the others. The moment WindowDispatcher begins tracking focus, z-order, or the state of live windows, it has become a manager — which it must never be.

# WindowInitContext

WindowDispatcher does not store raw factory callables. It stores WindowInitContext instances — lightweight objects that bundle two things together:

- **A window factory** — the callable that constructs the window envelope when invoked

- **A window descriptor** — a flags-based metadata object that governs the dispatch rules for this factory

The descriptor is what allows the dispatcher to make informed decisions at dispatch time without containing any hardcoded policy. Flags currently envisioned include a **single-instance flag** (this factory may not be dispatched if a live instance already exists) and a **main window flag** (this factory produces the application’s primary window).

When the main window flag is set, the dispatcher uses that factory to materialize the first window at runtime start. If no factory carries the flag, the first registered factory is used by default. The main window designation also carries behavioral weight at shutdown: most GUI frameworks will automatically initiate application exit when the main window closes, and Chevron respects that behavior rather than fighting it.

Enforcement of the single-instance constraint requires cooperation with WindowCoordinator, since only the coordinator has visibility into what windows are currently alive. The exact mechanism for that cooperation is a deferred design question.

# What WindowDispatcher Deliberately Does Not Own

*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*

WindowDispatcher does not own:

- The lifetime of any window it creates

- Knowledge of what windows are currently alive

- Focus, z-order, or any other live window state

- Shutdown logic or teardown sequencing

- Any GUI-framework-specific construction details

Once a window envelope leaves WindowDispatcher and enters WindowCoordinator, the dispatcher has no further knowledge of or authority over it.

# Lifetime of WindowDispatcher

WindowDispatcher is constructed as part of GUIEngine at the base class level and is destroyed during GUI teardown. Its lifetime is entirely bounded by the GUI engine that owns it.

*The dispatcher exists before windows, during window creation, and after windows — but windows only exist during one slice of its lifetime.*

That asymmetry is intentional. The dispatcher is not defined by the windows it has created. It is defined by its readiness to create them.

# Lifecycle of WindowDispatcher

The dispatcher moves through three distinct operational phases. Each phase has different rules about what is and is not legal. An internal phase state governs these transitions and makes the rules enforceable rather than merely documented.

## 1. Construction and Registration

Constructed as part of GUIEngine during the engine’s own construction. No GUI framework calls have occurred. The dispatcher is ready to accept WindowFactory registrations.

Factory registration is a pre-commitment activity. User code declares window intent through WindowingSubsystem via engine.windowing() before committing the engine to AppProcess. At commitment, the process-level registration window closes and the factory set is effectively locked. Post-commitment registration from within the GUI layer is an intentionally deferred capability and is not part of the current design.

*Factories registered here are declarative intent, not execution. No windows are created yet.*

## 2. Runtime Activation

When AppProcess calls mainloopEntry(), the dispatcher transitions to its active phase. This is the first moment at which dispatch requests are legal.

The dispatcher immediately materializes the startup window — either the factory carrying the main window flag, or the first registered factory if no flag is set — and hands the resulting envelope to WindowCoordinator. The mainloop then enters.

## 3. Active Runtime Dispatching

WindowDispatcher is not a one-time startup mechanism. During normal runtime operation, dispatch requests may arrive at any time — from user interaction, application logic, or internal triggers. The dispatcher handles each request uniformly: consult the descriptor, verify constraints, execute the factory if permitted, hand off the result.

For factories carrying the single-instance flag, the dispatcher consults WindowCoordinator to determine whether a live instance already exists before proceeding. Factories without this flag may be dispatched freely, producing as many instances as requested.

## 4. Shutdown

When GUI shutdown begins, the dispatcher transitions to its inert phase. Dispatch requests are immediately invalid. No new windows may be created. Existing windows are wound down by WindowCoordinator as part of the engine’s teardown sequence.

*Any dispatch attempt after shutdown has begun is a programming error and must be caught.*

# Error Handling Philosophy

WindowDispatcher should:

- Fail fast on any dispatch attempt outside of the active phase

- Refuse dispatch requests that violate descriptor constraints

- Never silently swallow a misuse — every violation must surface

**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as AppProcess and GUIEngine — deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

Examples of misuse that must be caught:

- Dispatch attempted before runtime activation

- Dispatch attempted after shutdown has begun

- Single-instance dispatch when a live instance already exists

- Dispatch against an unregistered or invalid factory key

# Open Questions and Deferred Decisions

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **WindowDispatcher**** / ****WindowCoordinator**** handoff mechanism: **The precise protocol by which a newly constructed window envelope transfers from the dispatcher to the coordinator has not been designed. This is the first question to resolve when these two classes are formalized together.

- **Single-instance constraint enforcement: **The dispatcher must consult WindowCoordinator to verify whether a live instance exists before honoring a single-instance dispatch request. The exact query interface between the two classes is deferred.

- **Post-commitment registration: **The ability for components inside the running GUI layer to register additional window factories after engine commitment is a deferred capability. The mechanism for providing safe, scoped access to the dispatcher from within the GUI environment has not been designed.

- **Error handling boundary: **Follows the same open question as AppProcess and GUIEngine. Deferred pending library-wide decisions.

**chevron::process::WindowFactory**

*Class Design Description*

# **What WindowFactory Is**

WindowFactory is the **unit of window registration** — the object a user constructs and submits to WindowDispatcher to declare that a particular kind of window exists in the application and describe the rules under which it may be created.

It bundles exactly two things: a **factory callable** that produces a WindowEnvelope when invoked, and a **descriptor** that governs the dispatch policy for that callable. Together they give the dispatcher everything it needs to decide whether a window may be created and how to create it, without the dispatcher itself containing any hardcoded policy.

It is not:

- A window instance or a handle to one

- A manager or tracker of any kind

- Responsible for enforcing its own descriptor constraints

- Aware of whether it has ever been dispatched

# **Where WindowFactory Sits in the Layering Model**

WindowFactory is a registration-time value type. It does not live at a specific layer in the runtime hierarchy — it exists only as a stored entry inside WindowDispatcher, whose lifetime it shares for as long as the dispatcher holds it.

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

                          |- WindowDispatcher   (creation authority)

                          |    |- WindowFactory (registered entry)

                          |    |- WindowFactory (registered entry)

                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)

                          |- WindowingSubsystem  (user-facing projection)

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

A WindowFactory is submitted by user code during the registration phase, assigned a dispatcher-managed ID, and stored. From that point forward it is owned and consulted exclusively by WindowDispatcher. User code retains no ongoing relationship with the WindowFactory after registration — its job is done at submission time.

# **What Problem WindowFactory Is Solving**

Without a structured registration type, WindowDispatcher would have no clean way to separate *what to create* from *the rules around creating it*. A raw callable answers the first question but says nothing about the second. Attaching policy directly to the dispatcher would require it to know about every kind of window it might manage — which violates its responsibility boundary.

WindowFactory solves this by making the pairing of construction logic and dispatch policy an explicit, named thing. The descriptor travels with the callable so the dispatcher never has to infer or assume anything — it reads the descriptor and acts accordingly. Policy stays with the registration, not with the mechanism that executes it.

# **Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)**

WindowFactory has exactly two responsibilities:

- **1.  **Hold the factory callable that produces a WindowEnvelope when invoked

- **2.  **Carry the descriptor that declares the dispatch policy for that callable

*Nothing else. WindowFactory is a value type, not a service. It does not act — it is consulted.*

# **What WindowFactory Carries**

## **The Factory Callable**

The callable is a user-supplied function or functor with a fixed signature. It accepts a single WindowInitContext parameter — the initialization token assembled by Chevron at dispatch time — and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>. The unique_ptr return makes ownership transfer explicit: the moment the factory call completes, the resulting envelope belongs to whoever receives it, which in practice is always WindowCoordinator via the dispatcher.

The WindowInitContext parameter is not constructed by user code. Chevron assembles it at dispatch time and passes it in. Its purpose is to provide the envelope with everything it needs to bootstrap Chevron’s own per-window infrastructure unconditionally, and to carry the parent window handle for subsidiary window dispatches — the one piece of information user code cannot obtain any other way. The full design of WindowInitContext is covered in its own dedicated class description document.

## **The Descriptor**

The descriptor is a lightweight flags type — a named bitmask — that declares the dispatch policy for this factory. Flags are composed with bitwise OR (|) at registration time and read by the dispatcher at dispatch time. The descriptor contains no logic of its own; it is pure metadata.

Flags currently envisioned:

- **Root window flag: **This factory produces the application’s primary root window, which corresponds to WindowKind::TOP_LEVEL. The dispatcher uses this to select the startup window when the mainloop begins. If no factory carries this flag, the first registered factory is used by default. Most GUI frameworks will automatically initiate application exit when the root window closes, and Chevron respects that behavior.

- **Subsidiary window flag: **This factory always produces a subsidiary window, which corresponds to WindowKind::SUBSIDIARY. Every dispatch request against this factory must carry a parent instance ID. Any dispatch that does not provide one is caught as a misuse immediately.

- **Single-instance flag: **This factory may not be dispatched if a live window envelope produced by it already exists. Enforcement requires the dispatcher to consult WindowCoordinator by factory ID before proceeding.

- **Minimum PWI flag: **This factory produces windows that require only the minimum viable per-window infrastructure. Signals to the envelope construction pathway that the full base component set should not be initialized. The precise definition of that minimum is deferred to the PWI design phase.

The flag set is finite and known at design time. A builder pattern would be unnecessary overhead for a type this constrained — direct flag composition with bitwise OR (|) is the right level of ceremony here.

# **Dispatcher-Assigned Identity**

When a WindowFactory is submitted to WindowDispatcher, the dispatcher assigns it a sequential numeric ID. This ID is the factory’s stable identity for the duration of the GUI lifetime. It is not chosen by user code — it is assigned at registration time and returned to the caller, who may capture it as a named constant for use in targeted dispatch requests.

The assigned ID serves two purposes:

- **Targeted dispatch: **User code or internal logic can request dispatch of a specific window by referencing its factory ID directly, rather than relying on positional or type-based lookup.

- **Single-instance enforcement: **Every WindowEnvelope produced by a factory carries that factory’s ID. When a single-instance dispatch is requested, the dispatcher asks WindowCoordinator whether any live envelope currently carries that ID. If one exists, dispatch is refused. This keeps the coordination interface between WindowDispatcher and WindowCoordinator narrow — a simple membership query by ID is all that is needed.

*The ID is assigned by the dispatcher, not stored inside the *WindowFactory* itself. The factory is submitted, the ID is returned. The association between ID and factory is the dispatcher’s concern, not the factory’s.*

# **What WindowFactory Deliberately Does Not Own**

*This boundary is just as important as what it does carry.*

WindowFactory does not own:

- Knowledge of whether it has ever been dispatched

- Knowledge of what windows it has produced

- Its own dispatch ID — that belongs to the dispatcher’s registry

- Any enforcement logic — the descriptor declares policy, the dispatcher enforces it

- Any reference to WindowCoordinator or the windows currently alive

WindowFactory is inert between dispatch invocations. It holds its callable and its descriptor and does nothing else.

# **Error Handling Philosophy**

Because WindowFactory is a value type with no lifecycle of its own, most error handling responsibility falls on WindowDispatcher rather than on WindowFactory itself. However, a WindowFactory submitted without a valid callable is a construction error and must be caught at registration time rather than deferred to dispatch time.

Construction errors that must be caught:

- Submitting a WindowFactory with a null or empty callable

- Submitting a WindowFactory with a contradictory descriptor (e.g. flags that are mutually exclusive, if any such combinations are defined)

**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library — deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

# **Open Questions and Deferred Decisions**

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **Factory callable type: **The precise C++ type used to store the callable — whether std::function, a raw function pointer, a concept-constrained template parameter, or something else — is deferred pending broader decisions on Chevron’s callable conventions.

- **Descriptor flag set completeness: **The four flags described here (root window, subsidiary window, single-instance, minimum PWI) represent the currently known set. Additional flags may be introduced as the dispatch model matures.

- **Mutually exclusive flag combinations: **Whether any combinations of descriptor flags are logically contradictory, and how those are detected and reported, has not been defined.

- **Post-commitment registration: **The mechanism by which WindowFactory instances may be registered from within the running GUI layer after engine commitment is a deferred capability, consistent with the same open question in WindowDispatcher.

- **Error handling boundary: **Follows the same open question as AppProcess, GUIEngine, and WindowDispatcher. Deferred pending library-wide decisions.

**chevron::process::WindowCoordinator**

*Class Design Description*

# **What WindowCoordinator Is**

WindowCoordinator is the **lifetime authority for all live window envelopes**. Where WindowDispatcher governs the act of creation, WindowCoordinator governs everything that follows: ownership, identity, relationships, and eventual teardown.

It is the single source of truth about what windows currently exist within the application. Every live WindowEnvelope is under its care from the moment the dispatcher hands one over to the moment the GUI shuts down.

It is not:

- A window factory or creation mechanism

- A GUI abstraction layer or event router

- A dispatcher or policy enforcer

- Directly accessible to user code — it operates entirely within GUIEngine's internal boundary

# **Where WindowCoordinator Sits in the Layering Model**

WindowCoordinator lives inside GUIEngine at the base class level alongside WindowDispatcher. Like the dispatcher, it is framework-agnostic infrastructure written once and shared across all concrete backend implementations.

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)

                          |    |- WindowFactory  (registered entry)

                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)

                          |    |- WindowHierarchy (relationship graph)

                          |- WindowingSubsystem  (user-facing projection)

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

The division between WindowDispatcher and WindowCoordinator is a clean handoff at the moment of creation: the dispatcher produces a WindowEnvelope and immediately transfers ownership to the coordinator. From that point forward the dispatcher has no knowledge of or authority over that envelope. The coordinator has full authority over it until shutdown.

The coordinator is not exposed outside of GUIEngine. All user-facing interaction with window state — including subsidiary window parenting — passes through WindowingSubsystem via engine.windowing(), which orchestrates the coordinator and dispatcher together as needed.

# **What Problem WindowCoordinator Is Solving**

Once a window exists, something has to own it, track it, understand its relationships to other windows, and know when it has gone away. Without a dedicated authority for this, that responsibility scatters — into the dispatcher, into the engine, into user code — and the system loses its ability to reason cleanly about window state.

WindowCoordinator centralizes all of that. It is the answer to every question of the form *“what windows exist right now?”* — whether that question comes from the dispatcher checking a single-instance constraint, from GUIEngine orchestrating a subsidiary window relationship, or from the shutdown sequence needing to wind down envelopes in the correct order.

# **Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)**

WindowCoordinator has exactly four responsibilities:

- **1.  **Receive and own WindowEnvelope instances transferred from WindowDispatcher

- **2.  **Assign each envelope a unique instance ID and maintain the registry of all live envelopes

- **3.  **Own and delegate to WindowHierarchy for all window relationship tracking

- **4.  **Detect significant window lifecycle events — particularly last-window-closed — and surface them to GUIEngine

*Nothing else. If a responsibility does not clearly fit into one of those buckets, it does not belong here.*

# **What WindowCoordinator Owns**

## **The Live Envelope Registry**

The coordinator maintains the authoritative registry of all live WindowEnvelope instances, keyed by their unique instance ID. This registry is the runtime answer to “what windows currently exist.”

Each envelope in the registry carries two IDs: its own unique **instance ID**, assigned by the coordinator at the moment of receipt, and the **factory ID** of the WindowFactory that produced it, embedded at dispatch time. The instance ID identifies the specific live window. The factory ID identifies the kind of window it is. Both are stable for the lifetime of the envelope.

The registry supports two natural query patterns that fall directly out of this dual-ID structure:

- **Lookup by instance ID: **Retrieve a specific live envelope directly. Used for targeted operations such as resolving a parent handle during subsidiary window construction.

- **Filter by factory ID: **Retrieve all live envelopes that were produced by a given factory. Used for single-instance enforcement and for any application logic that wants to reason about all open windows of a particular kind.

## **WindowHierarchy**

The coordinator owns a WindowHierarchy instance that maintains the parent-child relationship graph across all live envelopes. This is a dedicated type rather than data scattered across individual envelopes, keeping relationship logic centralized and the coordinator’s own code readable.

Relationships are tracked by instance ID. A parent envelope maps to a collection of child instance IDs, supporting the one-to-many cardinality that GUI window hierarchies naturally exhibit. Individual envelopes carry no relationship data themselves — the graph lives entirely inside WindowHierarchy.

Chevron does not attempt to manage window lifetime cascades directly. GUI frameworks handle the destruction of subsidiary windows when their parent closes, provided the windows were composed correctly at construction time. WindowHierarchy’s role is to keep Chevron’s own bookkeeping consistent after the framework has acted — not to duplicate or compete with what the framework already does well.

# **Instance Identity Assignment**

When the coordinator receives a new WindowEnvelope from the dispatcher, its first act is to assign that envelope a unique sequential instance ID. This ID is the envelope’s stable identity within Chevron for its entire lifetime.

Instance IDs and factory IDs serve different purposes and must not be confused. A factory ID identifies a registration — it is fixed at WindowFactory submission time and shared by every envelope that factory ever produces. An instance ID identifies a specific live window — it is assigned at receipt time and unique across all envelopes regardless of which factory produced them.

This distinction is what makes the single-instance query clean: the dispatcher asks the coordinator whether any live envelope carries a given *factory* ID. The coordinator answers by scanning its registry. No instance ID is involved in that query — only the factory ID embedded in each envelope at dispatch time.

# **Relationship to WindowDispatcher**

The coordinator is aware of the dispatcher but the dispatcher is not aware of the coordinator. This one-way dependency is intentional.

The dispatcher’s only need to reach the coordinator is to verify single-instance constraints before firing a factory. This is achieved through a narrow query interface — likely dependency-injected by GUIEngine at construction time — that exposes nothing beyond a simple membership check: “does any live envelope carry this factory ID?” The dispatcher calls this query and receives a yes or no. It has no further visibility into the coordinator’s state.

The coordinator, by contrast, is a full participant in the window lifecycle. It receives envelopes, maintains the registry, owns the hierarchy, and surfaces lifecycle events. Its awareness of the dispatcher is structural — it understands that envelopes arrive from a dispatcher — but it does not hold a reference to the dispatcher or call into it.

# **Relationship to GUIEngine**

The coordinator operates entirely within GUIEngine’s internal boundary. User code does not interact with it directly. All user-initiated operations that require coordinator involvement — querying live windows, establishing parent-child relationships, responding to window closure events — pass through WindowingSubsystem via engine.windowing(). Internal operations driven by GUIEngine’s own lifecycle — such as last-window-close signals — bypass the subsystem and are handled by the engine directly.

This is particularly relevant for subsidiary window construction. When user code requests a subsidiary window through WindowingSubsystem, GUIEngine resolves the parent envelope via the coordinator, assembles the WindowInitContext with the parent’s underlying window handle, and instructs the dispatcher to fire. The coordinator then receives the new envelope, registers it, and records the parent-child relationship in WindowHierarchy. The coordinator never reaches out to perform this orchestration itself — that belongs to the engine.

# **Lifecycle Event Awareness**

The coordinator is the component best positioned to detect meaningful window lifecycle events because it has visibility over the full population of live envelopes at all times.

The most significant event is last-window-closed. When the final envelope leaves the registry — whether because the root window closed and the framework initiated shutdown, or because the application explicitly destroyed all windows — the coordinator surfaces this to GUIEngine, which may in turn signal AppProcess to begin the shutdown sequence.

The coordinator does not initiate shutdown itself. It observes, records, and notifies. The decision of what to do in response to a lifecycle event belongs to GUIEngine and ultimately to AppProcess.

# **Shutdown and Teardown**

*Teardown is not the inverse of construction.*

When GUIEngine begins its shutdown sequence, the coordinator winds down all live envelopes in a controlled order. Subsidiary windows are addressed before their parents to avoid acting against what the framework has already handled. WindowHierarchy provides the traversal order.

Once an envelope has been wound down, it is removed from the registry and its entry in WindowHierarchy is cleared. The coordinator’s state is fully drained before GUIEngine proceeds with framework deinitialization.

At the end of teardown, no envelopes remain. The coordinator is empty but still valid — it does not destroy itself. Its lifetime is governed by the GUIEngine that owns it.

# **Error Handling Philosophy**

WindowCoordinator should:

- Fail fast on any operation that assumes a live envelope that does not exist in the registry

- Never silently drop an envelope or allow one to leak outside the registry

- Refuse any post-shutdown registration or query that implies new window activity

- Surface lifecycle events reliably — a missed last-window-closed notification is a correctness failure

**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library — deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

# **Open Questions and Deferred Decisions**

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **WindowDispatcher / WindowCoordinator handoff mechanism: **The precise protocol by which a newly constructed WindowEnvelope transfers ownership from the dispatcher to the coordinator — including the exact call sequence and any synchronization requirements — has not been designed.

- **Single-instance query interface: **The narrow interface through which WindowDispatcher queries the coordinator for factory ID membership has not been formally defined. The shape is clear — a boolean membership check by factory ID — but the precise C++ surface is deferred.

- **WindowHierarchy design: **The internal structure of WindowHierarchy — how the parent-to-children mapping is stored, how traversal order is determined at teardown, and what query API it exposes to the coordinator — is deferred to dedicated design work on that type.

- **Lifecycle event notification mechanism: **How the coordinator surfaces events such as last-window-closed to GUIEngine has not been defined. Candidates include callbacks, an observer interface, or a direct method call on GUIEngine. This is deferred pending broader decisions on Chevron’s internal event and notification patterns.

- **Framework cascade verification: **The mechanism by which Chevron verifies that the underlying framework has correctly handled subsidiary window teardown before cleaning up coordinator records has not been designed.

- **Error handling boundary: **Follows the same open question as AppProcess, GUIEngine, WindowDispatcher, and WindowFactory. Deferred pending library-wide decisions.

**chevron::process::WindowHierarchy**

*Class Design Description*

# **What WindowHierarchy Is**

WindowHierarchy is the **authoritative record of parent-child relationships between live window envelopes**. It is a focused data structure with a focused API — its sole concern is knowing which windows are related, in what direction, and in what order they should be addressed when relationships are dissolved.

It does not track window state, manage lifetimes, or interact with the GUI framework. It knows only about relationships between instance IDs, and it answers questions about those relationships cleanly and without side effects.

It is not:

- A window manager or lifetime authority

- A replacement for or competitor to the framework’s own parent-child window model

- Aware of the underlying framework window handles or any GUI-specific details

- Directly accessible to user code

# **Where WindowHierarchy Sits in the Layering Model**

WindowHierarchy is an internal component owned by WindowCoordinator. It does not sit at a named layer boundary in Chevron’s lifetime hierarchy — it is a focused sub-component that the coordinator delegates relationship concerns to, keeping that logic self-contained and its own code readable.

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)

                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)

                          |    |- WindowHierarchy (relationship graph)

                          |- WindowingSubsystem  (user-facing projection)

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

This nesting is deliberate. Relationship tracking is a specific sub-concern of the coordinator’s broader responsibility. Keeping it inside a dedicated type means the coordinator can answer relationship queries through a clean API rather than managing graph state inline. It also means WindowHierarchy can evolve independently if relationship tracking needs grow more complex over time.

# **What Problem WindowHierarchy Is Solving**

GUI applications composed of multiple windows inevitably have relationships between them. A subsidiary window belongs to a parent. When that parent is closed, the framework handles the cascade — but Chevron still needs to keep its own bookkeeping consistent. Without a dedicated structure for tracking those relationships, that logic either scatters into the coordinator’s general registry management or gets pushed onto individual envelopes, neither of which is clean.

WindowHierarchy solves this by giving relationship knowledge a single home. The coordinator registers relationships here when subsidiary windows are created and queries here during teardown to determine the correct order for winding down envelopes. The graph is always consistent with what the coordinator’s live registry contains because the two are updated together.

*WindowHierarchy does not manage window lifetimes. It records the relationships that the coordinator needs to reason about them correctly.*

# **Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)**

WindowHierarchy has exactly three responsibilities:

- **1.  **Record parent-child relationships between window instance IDs when subsidiary windows are registered

- **2.  **Answer relationship queries from WindowCoordinator — children of a given parent, whether a relationship exists, whether a window is a root

- **3.  **Provide a safe teardown traversal order that addresses children before parents

*Nothing else. WindowHierarchy is a data structure with a query API, not a service with behavior of its own.*

# **How Relationships Are Represented**

Relationships are stored as mappings between instance IDs. A parent instance ID maps to a collection of child instance IDs, supporting the one-to-many cardinality that window hierarchies naturally require. A window with no registered parent is a top-level window in the graph. A window with no children is a leaf.

No pointers to WindowEnvelope instances are held inside WindowHierarchy. This is a deliberate choice. Instance IDs are stable, non-owning references that cannot dangle. Holding pointers would create lifetime coupling between the hierarchy and the envelopes it describes, which would complicate teardown sequencing and make the coordinator’s ownership story harder to reason about.

Individual envelopes carry no relationship data themselves. They know their own instance ID and the factory ID they were produced from, but nothing about their position in the relationship graph. The graph lives entirely inside WindowHierarchy and is the coordinator’s concern alone.

# **Relationship to the Framework’s Own Hierarchy**

Most GUI frameworks natively support the concept of parent and subsidiary windows, and handle lifetime cascade automatically when a parent window closes — provided windows were composed correctly at construction time. Chevron embraces this behavior rather than duplicating it.

WindowHierarchy is not a replacement for the framework’s own relationship model. It is Chevron’s mirror of that model, maintained in terms that Chevron can reason about. When the framework closes subsidiary windows as a consequence of a parent closing, WindowHierarchy is consulted to keep the coordinator’s registry consistent with what the framework has already done — not to drive the cascade itself.

The only case where Chevron would need to act on hierarchy data to manage cascade manually is if a particular GUI framework does not handle subsidiary window teardown automatically. This is expected to be rare and is a deferred consideration.

# **Teardown Traversal Order**

During GUIEngine shutdown, WindowCoordinator asks WindowHierarchy for a safe order in which to wind down live envelopes. The rule is consistent: children are always addressed before their parents. This ensures that no envelope is wound down while another live envelope still holds it as a registered parent.

The traversal is a post-order walk of the relationship graph — leaf nodes first, windows with no registered parent addressed last. For windows with no registered relationships, order relative to other parentless windows is unspecified and does not matter.

As each envelope is wound down during this sequence, its entry is removed from WindowHierarchy alongside its removal from the coordinator’s live registry. The two structures are always kept in sync.

# **Lifetime of WindowHierarchy**

WindowHierarchy is constructed as part of WindowCoordinator and destroyed when the coordinator is destroyed. Its lifetime is entirely bounded by the coordinator that owns it. It holds no resources beyond its own relationship data and requires no special teardown beyond clearing that data, which happens naturally as envelopes are wound down during the shutdown sequence.

At the end of a clean shutdown, WindowHierarchy is empty. Any entries remaining at that point would indicate envelopes that were not properly wound down — a coordinator-level correctness failure.

# **What WindowHierarchy Deliberately Does Not Own**

*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*

WindowHierarchy does not own:

- Any WindowEnvelope instance or pointer

- Knowledge of window state, visibility, focus, or any runtime GUI property

- Any framework window handle or backend-specific reference

- The logic for deciding when or whether a relationship should exist — that belongs to GUIEngine

- Teardown execution — it provides traversal order, WindowCoordinator acts on it

# **Error Handling Philosophy**

WindowHierarchy should:

- Refuse to register a relationship where the parent instance ID is not known to the coordinator

- Refuse to register a relationship that would create a cycle

- Fail fast if queried for children of an instance ID that does not exist in the graph

- Never silently produce an incomplete or inconsistent traversal order

**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library — deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

# **Open Questions and Deferred Decisions**

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **Internal graph representation: **The precise data structure used to store the parent-to-children mapping — whether an adjacency list, a map of sets, or another form — is an implementation detail deferred to development.

- **Cycle detection strategy: **How and when cycles are detected during relationship registration has not been defined. Whether this is checked eagerly on every registration or lazily during traversal is an open question.

- **Query API completeness: **The full set of queries WindowCoordinator will need from WindowHierarchy — beyond children-of, root-check, and teardown traversal — will become clearer as the coordinator’s implementation matures. Additional query methods may be introduced.

- **Manual cascade handling: **The mechanism by which Chevron handles subsidiary window teardown for frameworks that do not automatically cascade on parent close is deferred. WindowHierarchy’s traversal order is the foundation for this but the driving logic has not been designed.

- **Error handling boundary: **Follows the same open question as the rest of the library. Deferred pending library-wide decisions.

**chevron::process::WindowEnvelope**

*Class Design Description*

# **What WindowEnvelope Is**

WindowEnvelope is the **per-window infrastructure (PWI) container** that represents a single live window within Chevron’s runtime. It bundles the raw backend window handle produced by a user-supplied factory with the identity, lifecycle machinery, and per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides unconditionally for every window it governs.

It is not the framework window itself. It is the structure that surrounds that window — giving it a stable identity within Chevron, a home for its infrastructure, and a handle through which every upstream class in the system can reason about it uniformly regardless of what GUI framework is underneath.

It is not inheritable. Extensibility is provided through WindowComponentStore, the typed component container the envelope owns. User code never subclasses WindowEnvelope — it extends what lives inside it.

It is not:

- The backend window object or a wrapper around its API

- A window manager or event router

- User-constructible directly — Chevron owns the construction pathway

- A base class for user-defined window types

# **Where WindowEnvelope Sits in the Layering Model**

WindowEnvelope occupies the innermost named layer of Chevron’s lifetime hierarchy. Every instance is produced by WindowDispatcher via a factory call and immediately transferred to WindowCoordinator, which owns it for the remainder of its lifetime. The envelope exists only while the GUI engine is active.

Process lifetime   ->   AppProcess

GUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine

                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)

                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)

                          |    |- WindowHierarchy (relationship graph)

                          |- WindowingSubsystem  (user-facing projection)

Window lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope

                          |- WindowComponentStore (PWI components)

The envelope is the unit of currency in Chevron’s window layer. Every operation that WindowCoordinator performs — tracking, querying, teardown ordering — is performed on envelopes. Every operation that GUIEngine orchestrates — subsidiary window parenting, shutdown sequencing, lifecycle event propagation — is performed through envelopes. The uniform handle the envelope provides is what allows upstream classes to reason about any window without knowing anything about the underlying framework.

# **What Problem WindowEnvelope Is Solving**

Without a uniform per-window container, Chevron has no clean way to associate its own infrastructure with a live window. The framework window handle is a raw pointer with no Chevron semantics attached. The coordinator can track it by address, but it cannot ask it for a logging context, a memory arena, or a viewport system — because those things have nowhere to live.

WindowEnvelope solves this by being the place those things live. It gives every window a stable Chevron identity and a structured home for per-window infrastructure. Because the envelope is always present and always uniformly structured, any Chevron subsystem can reach into any live window’s envelope and reliably find the components it needs — without knowing anything about the specific window, its factory, or the framework behind it.

This is the mechanism by which per-window infrastructure becomes a first-class library feature rather than something each application has to wire up manually.

# **Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)**

WindowEnvelope has exactly four responsibilities:

- **1.  **Hold the raw backend window handle for the duration of the window’s lifetime

- **2.  **Carry the identity information Chevron assigns — instance ID, factory ID, and window kind

- **3.  **Own the WindowComponentStore and guarantee base components are populated unconditionally at construction

- **4.  **Expose a lifecycle hook surface that Chevron’s internal infrastructure can bind into

*Nothing else. The envelope is a structured container with a governed lifetime, not a service or a policy class.*

# **What WindowEnvelope Carries**

## **The Backend Window Handle**

The raw handle to the framework window — a wxFrame*, a QMainWindow*, or equivalent — produced by the user’s factory callable. This is the one genuinely framework-specific piece inside an otherwise framework-agnostic structure. It is required and always present. Its lifetime is governed by the envelope: Chevron owns the handle from the moment the envelope is constructed and is responsible for its destruction during teardown.

## **Identity**

The envelope carries three stable identity values, all set at construction and immutable for the envelope’s lifetime:

- **Instance ID: **A unique sequential identifier assigned by WindowCoordinator at the moment it takes ownership of the envelope. This is the envelope’s identity within Chevron — the handle by which upstream classes target operations against this specific live window.

- **Factory ID: **The identifier of the WindowFactory that produced this envelope, embedded at dispatch time. This identifies the kind of window this envelope represents and is used by WindowCoordinator for single-instance queries and by-factory filtering.

- **Window kind: **A WindowKind enumeration value — either TOP_LEVEL or SUBSIDIARY — set at dispatch time based on how the factory was dispatched. This is structural information, not a runtime state. A TOP_LEVEL window has no parent. A SUBSIDIARY window was dispatched with a declared parent and its backend window was constructed with that parent relationship made real through the framework.

## **WindowComponentStore**

The envelope owns a WindowComponentStore — a type-keyed component container that holds all per-window infrastructure associated with this window instance. Each component is a distinct named type. Components are stored under std::type_index keys and retrieved by type, with no shared base class required.

Chevron populates a set of **base components** unconditionally at construction time for every envelope. These are the pieces of per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides as a matter of course — things like a memory arena scoped to window lifetime, a logging context tagged to this window, and dynamic view infrastructure. The precise base component set is defined by the PWI design phase and is deferred, but the pattern is fixed: base components are always present and their population is guaranteed by the construction pathway.

Beyond the base set, both Chevron subsystems and user code may register **optional components** at any point during the envelope’s lifetime. Optional components follow the same type-keyed storage model. Each type may only be registered once per envelope — a duplicate registration is a caught error. The store is internally synchronized with a mutex, making it safe for optional component registration to occur from any thread without the caller needing to coordinate access.

For windows where even the base component set is unnecessary overhead — transient dialogs, splash screens, lightweight utility windows — the **minimum PWI flag** on the WindowFactory descriptor signals that only the minimum viable infrastructure should be initialized. What “minimum viable” means precisely is a deferred PWI decision, but the mechanism for requesting it is settled at the descriptor level.

# **Construction Pathway**

User code does not construct WindowEnvelope directly. The constructor is not part of the public interface. Instead, Chevron provides a controlled construction function that is the only legitimate way to produce an envelope instance.

Inside a factory callable, the flow is:

- The factory receives a WindowInitContext assembled by Chevron at dispatch time

- The factory constructs the backend window instance using information from the WindowInitContext as needed — including the parent window handle for subsidiary windows, surfaced as a void* that the factory casts to the appropriate framework type

- The factory passes the backend window handle and the WindowInitContext to Chevron’s envelope construction function

- Chevron constructs the envelope internally, assigns identity, populates base components, and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>

- The factory returns that pointer, transferring ownership to WindowDispatcher, which immediately hands it to WindowCoordinator

This pathway ensures that no WindowEnvelope can exist without a valid WindowInitContext having been involved in its construction. The WindowInitContext is the authority token that makes the construction legitimate. Without it, there is no envelope.

# **What WindowEnvelope Deliberately Does Not Own**

*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*

WindowEnvelope does not own:

- Window state visible to the framework — focus, z-order, visibility, position. The framework owns that.

- Relationship data — no parent or child references live on the envelope. That is WindowHierarchy’s concern.

- Its own lifetime — that belongs to WindowCoordinator.

- Knowledge of other live envelopes or the state of the application’s window population.

- Any framework-specific API surface beyond holding the raw handle.

# **Lifetime of WindowEnvelope**

An envelope is born when WindowDispatcher fires a factory and transfers the result to WindowCoordinator. It lives for as long as WindowCoordinator holds it in its registry. It is destroyed when the coordinator winds it down — either as part of the shutdown sequence or in response to the underlying framework window being closed.

During teardown, the envelope’s components are destroyed in the reverse order of their registration. The backend window handle is released last. At the end of teardown, the envelope is removed from the coordinator’s registry and destroyed. Nothing may reference it after that point.

*An envelope’s lifetime is the window’s lifetime from Chevron’s perspective. When the envelope is gone, the window is gone.*

# **Error Handling Philosophy**

WindowEnvelope and its construction pathway should:

- Treat any attempt to construct an envelope outside of Chevron’s controlled construction pathway as a hard error

- Guarantee that base components are fully populated before the envelope is returned from construction — a partially initialized envelope must never escape

- Catch duplicate component registrations immediately and surface them as errors

- Fail fast on any attempt to access the component store after the envelope has begun teardown

**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library — deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.

# **Open Questions and Deferred Decisions**

The following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:

- **Base component set: **The precise set of components Chevron populates unconditionally in every envelope — which subsystems qualify, what they are named, and in what order they are initialized — is deferred to dedicated PWI design work. This is the primary area of remaining design depth for this class.

- **Minimum PWI flag effect: **The precise definition of what “minimum viable” infrastructure means when the minimum PWI flag is set — which base components are skipped and which are retained unconditionally — is deferred to the PWI design phase.

- **Backend window handle ownership semantics: **Whether Chevron destroys the backend window handle directly during teardown or signals the framework to do so, and how that varies per backend, has not been defined.

- **Lifecycle hook surface: **The precise shape of the lifecycle hooks the envelope exposes — on-create, on-destroy, and any intermediate hooks — and how Chevron’s internal infrastructure binds into them is deferred.
